paragraphs: From March to April 2024, through Nagoya University's overseas study program, I took part in a four-week clinical clerkship in medical oncology at Duke University Hospital. For me, interested in the treatment of and research on solid tumors, the medical oncology clerkship at Duke University, a first-class academic institution, was a very valuable experience.

Duke University is located in Durham, North Carolina, and is among the top universities in the United States. Durham once prospered on the tobacco and textile industries, but since the Research Triangle Park (RTP) was established in the 1950s, it has become known as a university town that hosts Duke University. RTP is a vast research and development hub surrounded by three cities, Durham, Raleigh and Chapel Hill, and is now a center of high-tech industry, biotechnology and medical research, among the leading in the United States. Durham, influenced by the Research Triangle Park, has developed as a place of innovation, but at the same time it is also a quiet, peaceful town rich in nature, and in the garden of the host family where I stayed there were squirrels and birds too, so it was a quiet and very comfortable town.

Duke University is known as a pioneer of bone marrow transplantation for leukemia, and it carries out cutting-edge treatment and research, such as Gleevec for patients with CML and, recently, clinical trials changing the treatment drugs for HER2-positive breast cancer, and it is highly evaluated worldwide. I was fortunate to have the opportunity to do a four-week clerkship in such a luxurious environment.

I mainly helped with ward work and, in my free time, took part in the outpatient clinics of doctors I was interested in. The typical flow of a day on the ward alone was: 5:30 arrive on the ward and check patients; 7:00 handover from the night shift; 8:00 student rounds, making an assessment and plan; 10:00 presentation to the supervising doctor when free, plus guidance from the doctor; 13:00 shadowing a fellow; 16:00 the fellow goes home, and I do homework and update patients; 17:00 end.

In the assessment and plan, I was required to predict prognosis using papers as evidence. The ward where I did my clerkship was medical oncology, which specializes in the medical treatment of cancer, and it was not enough to simply read out the guideline; I had to refer to the literature of the clinical studies underlying the guideline, evaluate whether the patient met the requirements of that study, and how well progression-free survival and remission rates could be predicted from that study. Furthermore, when there was no study to refer to, I was required to infer the patient's prognosis from similar studies and tell the doctor with a clear explanation of the basis. Through this process, I was strongly made aware that current treatment is based on past research.

In time outside the ward, I made appointments directly with doctors I was interested in and took part in their outpatient clinics. What impressed me particularly was Professor Carey Anders, a medical oncologist for breast cancer. She is very careful in dealing with patients in the outpatient clinic, leads clinical trials and actively takes part in clinical research. She is also involved in basic research on breast cancer and genetic analysis, and is a wonderful doctor who serves as division chief of medical oncology while raising children. She is also trusted warmly by patients, who smile the moment they see Anders and end up talking a lot, even about trivial things. One cancer patient shed tears when told there was no standard treatment, but when Professor Anders said, "I can refer you to a doctor leading a clinical trial at another institution," the patient again shed tears, this time of joy. Unfortunately that patient did not take part in that trial, but I realized that her presence and the existence of the trial gave the patient hope to live. We healthcare professionals, in the case of advanced cancer, can anticipate the limits, such as the expected survival rates of trials, but I reaffirmed how great the impact of clinical trials on patients is, and I strongly felt I want to become a doctor like Dr. Anders who gives patients hope through advanced medicine.

On the ward and in the outpatient clinic, I took part in family meetings that proposed the hospice option to patients with no active cancer treatment and a short prognosis, and to their families. Not only the supervising doctors but also the resident doctors were skilled at delivering bad news such as cancer disclosure and hospice proposals, and when I asked why, it seemed they were accustomed to it because they had experienced such settings since their medical school days. I did not take part in such things in clerkships at Nagoya University, so it was a very valuable experience. For medical students every single case is special and in a sense they are in a protected environment, and I felt that having such psychologically burdensome experiences during this moratorium period is a very meaningful experience for becoming a doctor in the future who understands patients' feelings.

Comparing the oncology ward at Duke University with wards in Japan, the following points can be raised. 1. Comparison of treatment level: Apart from the abundance of clinical trials, there was no great difference in treatment level between Japan and Duke University, and they seemed almost equivalent. 2. Multidisciplinary cooperation and efficiency-oriented management: While in Japan doctors perform various tasks, at Duke University PAs (Physician Assistants), nurse practitioners and ward pharmacists each handle highly specialized work, and each shows strengths by complementing one another's knowledge, achieving a high level of treatment and efficient management. In fact, of the more than 50 supervising doctors in solid tumor oncology, only one medical oncology supervising doctor was in charge of the ward. 3. Doctors' working system: At Duke University the work of doctors who have obtained specialist qualifications is minimized, and they can devote much time to activities other than clinical work, such as research and education. In research, I also realized that funding and the environment for collaborative research are very favorable compared with Japan. 4. Educational staff: The staff at Duke University are educational, and every doctor, despite being very busy, took time to explain and give lessons.

On holidays I mainly enjoyed weekends with my host family and friends in the neighborhood. Every two weeks I took part in volunteer activities with Fred and Jenny, who looked after me as my host family, and spending time with kind-hearted people in rich nature cleansed my heart. One holiday I went to a Durham Bulls baseball game and enjoyed authentic baseball. Attending a concert by my friend Bridgett and being nearly moved to tears by her performance, having the chance to meet Prime Minister Kishida during his trip abroad and, when I said "I met the prime minister of Japan" to those around me, being arbitrarily recognized as someone great by various doctors, were all good memories that I would not have experienced in Japan. Above all, I was healed every day by the dog at my homestay, Bagger.

Dr. 原田洋平, an alumnus of Nagoya University's Frontier Society who now works at a pharmaceutical company near Duke University, welcomed me very warmly from the time I went to Durham, invited me to a home party, created opportunities for me to talk with Japanese researchers who had come to Duke and Chapel Hill, and gave me all kinds of support. In addition, I visited the laboratory of Dr. Batsis, a doctor in Chapel Hill who had previously come to Nagoya University, and met a doctor active as a cardiac surgeon at the University of Chicago, and learned the secrets of success in the United States.

The content of the training itself might be possible in Japan too. The ward work I did at Duke University, exhausting myself every day, is also what I would do in Japan once I become a resident, and I think Japanese residents surpass American medical students in both the quantity and quality of clinical work. Even so, I realize that I was glad I went to medical oncology at Duke University for the following two reasons.

Until now I had leaned toward results-orientation and had a self-centered way of thinking, that as long as I am fine, as long as those around me are fine, it is fine. However, through the preparation for this clerkship, I was helped many times by meetings with various people I had not expected and by their warm-hearted actions. Through this experience, I strongly felt that I want to become a person who can lend a hand to those in need.

As I spent my daily clerkship as an outsider, I placed myself in an environment where I had to convey every day who I am, what I came to learn and what I want to do. As a result, I was able to listen to my true feelings inside. In Japan, the title "medical student of Nagoya University" protects me, for better and for worse, but in the environment where I did my clerkship I felt firsthand that one is evaluated on one point only, "what can I contribute." In four weeks I could only just notice this for the future, but from now on I will find my own distinctive features and develop them.

My goal for the future is "to become an academic medical oncologist, contribute to the development of medicine, and become a person needed by everyone around me." I will continue to work hard, taking the wonderful experiences gained through the clerkship as nourishment.

Finally, I express my heartfelt gratitude to Dr. ブストス, who drilled the basics of medical education into me, Dr. 長谷川 and Dr. 粕谷, who coordinated my study abroad to the end, the doctors of the Frontier Society, who, despite being very busy, taught me the ABCs of clinical study abroad, my host family Jenny and Fred, who looked after me in Durham, Dr. 原田, the doctors of Duke including Dr. Anders and Dr. Matthew, and all the doctors who looked after me.
